chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Black stars not reviving older music; teachers courting popularity
summary: Hinton asks why white players revive Morton while Black stars do not; Maxwell blames teachers seeking popularity.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yet, to take the opposite side of what you say of events, I agree with you on events, the young black player, perhaps, he might be crowded. But now that we have schools and quite a number of our young black musicians are in school, and we have jazz workshops, we have some people -- we're beginning to get into that. But I find that some of our regular -- some of our popular black stars are not -- don't go back and do a Louis Armstrong song in 1979. I happen to remember hearing some black instrumentalist that had recently done something on shades of Bix. I haven't heard anybody doing

anything on Shades of Louis, some name players. You know, I don't want to throw anyone's name in particular, but I was wondering -- and yet we have some white players that have been doing some excellent jobs on recreating and reviving and bringing a rebirth to some of our great black composers, like Jelly Roll and some of great pianists. We know who they are. And I don't remember, recently, any of our name black artists doing this kind of thing. I was wondering what you think about that?

I think that you can't criticize the black teachers any more than you criticize white teachers, because all teachers nowadays, black or white in any subject, seem to be more interested in conducting a popularity contest with the young people rather than trying to direct them, which a teacher should be doing. Rather than trying to present them with something at first they may not want to know and then showing them the value of it, I think -- I'm talking about all teachers. My son is a teacher and I hear many stories about this anxiety to be popular with the pupils. And I think perhaps they resist doing that because they don't want to present something to the pupils that's going to cause a struggle at first. And I think that could be one explanation.
Because I know that the pupils -- and you know, if you talk about Louis Armstrong right away they say, oh, yeah, I know him, 'Hello, Dolly,' you know. And they don't know
anything about the dynamite stuff he did in the 20's and 30's.
